item.title: Changes Are Coming to the FAFSA. But Will It Be ‘Delightful’?
item.description:
Filling out the FAFSA college student aid form may not yet be “delightful,” as federal officials hope. But after fixes triggered by a notorious technical meltdown three years ago, the online application may start to shed its burdensome reputation.

The FAFSA update for the 2027-28 academic year is undergoing testing and is scheduled to be made widely available to students by Oct. 1, the traditional annual opening date.

“It has changed tremendously for the better,” said Julia Hellmich, senior managing director of the college readiness and alumni support program at KIPP DC, a network of charter schools in Washington. KIPP DC students participated in testing of the new form this month.

The new form can generally be completed quickly, and gives students an estimate of their financial aid eligibility much faster than previous versions did, according to Federal Student Aid officials as well as advocates and parents who have tested it.

A government website was upbeat, telling users, “There’s a lot to look forward to” in the new FAFSA. It said changes, like tweaks to the wording of some questions, “aim to make the applicant experience quicker and more delightful.”

That should be welcome news for families in a year that has brought worrisome changes to the world of student aid, including new borrowing limits on education loans for parents and graduate students.

The FAFSA now has a new feature, added in April for the current, 2026-27 form and kept for the coming October version, that could be off-putting for some students: embedded fraud detection screening, which could require some students to verify their identities on camera while completing the form.

Here’s what to know about this year’s form.

The FAFSA, short for the Free Application for Federal Student Aid, is required for students seeking federal financial aid for studies beyond high school. The form collects personal and financial information from students and parents and calculates eligibility for federal aid, including grants, work-study programs and low-cost loans.

Many states and many universities also use the form to divvy up their own need-based aid. About two million high school seniors typically file the form each year, according to the National College Attainment Network, a nonprofit that promotes college attendance. And research shows that high school seniors who complete the FAFSA are more likely to attend college right after graduation.

Yes, based on early trials of the form, known as beta testing. “It’s 99 percent running smoothly,” said Eddy Conroy, a spokesman for the National College Attainment Network. Several of the group’s member organizations have participated in the testing, which began in early August and expanded to a wider pool of students on Monday.

About 2,300 forms were completed in the first stage of beta testing, according to the Education Department, and larger numbers are going to be processed in the coming weeks.

Live testing of the form before its wide release has become routine as part of the effort to catch potential issues early. In the fall of 2023, during a major overhaul of the form under the Biden administration, serious glitches delayed the form’s availability by about three months. The situation improved in 2024 after early testing helped identify problems, but the form was still delayed by a month. Last fall, under the Trump administration, the FAFSA opened to the public on time.

Early testers were invited by community groups and schools chosen by the Education Department in seven states (Alabama, Arizona, California, Florida, Mississippi, New York and Pennsylvania) as well as in Washington, D.C., Puerto Rico and the Marshall Islands (which has close ties to the United States).

You can join the latest test phase by submitting a request online at StudentAid.gov. If you are chosen, you’ll be notified by email. If you complete the form during the testing period, you won’t need to resubmit it later; the forms filed during the test are official FAFSAs.

Financial aid experts say it’s fine to wait until October to complete the form. “There’s no advantage or disadvantage” to filing it before then, said Sarah Austin, a policy analyst at the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators — unless you want to cross a task off your to-do list. “If October is a significantly busy month for you, you can absolutely request to participate now,” she said.

Leslie Smith, 57, who lives in Washington and is a part-time student, said she and her daughter, a sophomore at American University, had each filled out the form at an event hosted by College Track, a group that promotes college readiness. “I like to get stuff off my plate,” Ms. Smith said. Because she had filled out the form before, she said, most of her information was already there. It took her less than 15 minutes to complete it.

Once the form opens to the public, it’s typically best to submit it as soon as you can, Ms. Austin said. That’s because states and colleges may have limited aid and often set priority deadlines for applications, some as early as mid-January. If you wait too long, you may miss out on money for college.

One welcome change is that students and families should get an estimate of their federal aid eligibility within a minute or two of submitting the form, Mr. Conroy said. Previously, they had to wait several days.

That’s a significant improvement, he said, because students and their parents often complete the form at evening or weekend workshops. With a swift response, they can discuss the results and head home with a better idea of how much aid they can expect for college, rather than having to follow up again later.

Overall, said Aaron Lemon-Strauss, the former FAFSA program director, the average time to complete a form is now about 10 minutes per person, based on data from the current FAFSA and the beta testing that reflects first-time and returning filers. In the past, he said, it could take an hour or longer.

Manisha Mishra, deputy director of Alabama Possible, a nonprofit antipoverty group that promotes college attendance, said 127 families attended its FAFSA test event on Aug. 20 at a high school in Trussville, Ala. Most completed the form in about 15 to 20 minutes, she said.

At KIPP DC, 175 students participated in testing this year, with 40 percent completing the form at an in-person event. That’s an increase from 20 percent last year, when KIPP DC first joined the testing, a spokesman said.

So-called real-time identity screening tools were added to the FAFSA in April to reduce student aid fraud, the Federal Student Aid department said. Based on the analysis of the built-in tools, participants considered “high risk” would be required to confirm their identities on camera by showing a government-issued ID, like a driver’s license. Factors used to assess risk might include mouse and keyboard movement that suggest automation, and whether the applicant’s location fits with his or her home and school addresses, according to a summary provided during a summit on higher-education fraud in July. The high-risk screening could affect about 3 percent of people filling out the FAFSA, officials have said.

item.title: The ‘Odyssey’ Scholar Emily Wilson, a Critic of the Movie, Is Redoing Her Translation
item.description:
Less than a decade after becoming the first woman to translate “The Odyssey” into English, Emily Wilson, the Homeric decoder who started an uproar in July when she panned Christopher Nolan’s movie adaptation, is retranslating the ancient Greek poem from scratch.

Wilson’s original interpretation became a best seller after it was released in 2017 by W.W. Norton & Company, presenting “The Odyssey” through what scholars said was a modern lens while remaining faithful to the poem written roughly 2,800 years ago.

Nolan cited Wilson’s translation as influencing his blockbuster movie. (That was before Wilson’s scathing criticism of the big-budget production in The London Review of Books.)

But in a highly unusual reboot, Wilson said in a statement on Friday that her translation would benefit from not just revisions, but a fresh start.

“I’m now retranslating ‘The Odyssey’ from scratch, with an approach closer to that of my translation of ‘The Iliad,’ using somewhat more lines than the original, enabling more varied word-length and pacing,” she said in the statement. “Also, I’ll have much more extensive end notes.”

The project, which Wilson said is a few years from completion, was reported earlier by The Associated Press.

“It’s always a huge privilege to get to spend all day reading Homer and wrestling with the endlessly fascinating challenges of how to convey ancient Greek into fluent English verse,” she said.

Wilson said she remained proud of her 2017 translation of “The Odyssey,” describing it as “conveying the rhythm, rapidity and freshness of Homeric poetics — features that are genuinely essential in the experience of the original Greek epics.”

Peter Simon, Wilson’s editor and the editor in chief of Liveright Publishing, an imprint of W.W. Norton & Company, said in a statement on Friday that the publishing house became excited when Wilson first mentioned the project.

“She has poured so much of her life and scholarship into ‘The Odyssey’ that her new approach is bound to be thrilling,” Simon said.

Wilson’s translation has sold more than a million copies since it was published, Simon said.

“We saw an uptick, though, as soon as the movie was announced, and a tremendous increase leading into, and following, the release of the film,” Simon added.

Katrine Øgaard Jensen, executive director of the American Literary Translators Association, said in an email on Friday that Wilson was venturing into somewhat uncharted territory.

“While it is common to tweak or edit an earlier version of a translation for new editions, it is fairly uncommon to retranslate your own already-published books in translation completely from scratch,” Øgaard Jensen said.

Still, such an undertaking is not entirely new.

In 2019, Ros Schwartz, a decorated translator of French fiction and nonfiction books, retranslated “I Who Have Never Known Men,” a dystopian novel by the Belgian author Jacqueline Harpman, Øgaard Jensen said.

Ms. Schwartz’s first translation came out in 1997.

Øgaard Jensen said she expects there will be an appetite for Wilson’s fresh interpretation of “The Odyssey.”

“Her first Odyssey translation was already a sensation — but I, for one, very much look forward to reading her new translation and everything that I know she’ll bring to it,” she said. “To me and countless others in our field, Wilson’s artistry and deep knowledge of her source material embodies the value of human literary translation.”

Treading on new scholarly ground might not be the sole consideration for such an endeavor. The opportunity to command additional income from book advances and sales can be an enticing one, particularly in the case of “The Odyssey,” one of the most translated books of all time.

Another example of that commercial success is “I Who Have Never Known Men,” which rose to prominence on BookTok, a subcommunity on TikTok where readers share videos reviewing and discussing books. The social media platform has expanded the footprint of many books and helped boost sales.

Wilson, who is department chairwoman of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania, appeared initially to welcome the renewed attention for “The Odyssey” that would accompany the movie’s release in July.

On a July 12 episode of “The Daily,” the podcast of The New York Times, said she was “pumped” to see how the tale played out on the big screen.

“I mean, it’s going to be exciting that so many people who may have thought, ‘Oh, ancient literature is boring, or it’s not for me, or it’s too inaccessible,’ are then going to realize, actually, this is a really compelling story,” Wilson said. “And some proportion of the people who go to the movie will then turn back to the original poem, which I think is great. I love that.”

Asked about purists potentially taking exception to Nolan’s artistic choices, Wilson said it would not be the first time that Homeric poems were adapted for performance.

“I think it’s totally fine and valid for a director to explore his own vision,” she said of Nolan.

But once she saw the movie, Wilson did not spare her criticism, writing that Nolan’s adaptation lacked many of the elements that made the poem great.

“It has nothing convincing to say about time, memory, history, war, or about the relationship between one warrior’s glorious return and the lives of his family, adversaries, comrades, friends and neighbors,” she wrote. “It lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth. Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal.”

Wilson argued that the movie embraced style over substance.

“It’s a family-friendly audiovisual spectacle, like an elaborate Fourth of July fireworks display — and with about the same level of narrative and emotional depth,” she wrote.

Wilson’s pointed commentary kindled a debate over balancing commercial success with literary authenticity, temporarily crashing the website of The London Review of Books.

Nolan, whose “Oppenheimer” won seven Academy Awards in 2024, including for best picture and best director, has not responded publicly to Wilson’s scathing review.

item.title: When Older Adults Choose Life Among the Young
item.description:
Q: I’m interested in areas where seniors can live alongside college students, and even younger kids, but I don’t know much about them. They’re called intergenerational living communities or university retirement communities. Are they located across the country? How affordable are they? What else should I know about them?

A: Communities where people of different generations live together intentionally have been gaining in popularity as a way for older adults to thrive in retirement and younger people to learn from those with more experience.

“It’s living in an engaged, less socially isolated way,” said Matthew Kaplan, a professor of intergenerational programs and aging at Pennsylvania State University.

University retirement communities, found on college campuses around the country, are a popular version of this kind of setting. The costs can be comparable to those of traditional senior living. They allow older adults to have a vibrant lifestyle while engaging in on-campus classes, performing arts and athletics.

“They do not want to live on Elderly Island,” said Andrew Carle, a senior living consultant and founder of UniversityRetirementCommunities.com, which offers information about such sites.

Other communities also allow for intergenerational living, with older adults living near families with children. Around the country, there are hundreds of “cohousing” developments, many of them designed to foster interaction among people of different age groups. In these, private housing units share indoor and outdoor spaces, and prices are comparable with other local housing. Generally speaking, intergenerational living can be market-rate, or subsidized.

Older adults interested in such living arrangements should consider how much interaction with others they’d like. Does the community allow people of different age groups to live near each other or together? Does the community offer programming aimed at promoting interaction? Is there a requirement to participate?

Be sure to be clear on financial terms: In intergenerational communities, arrangements can vary wildly, said Juli Ford, a real estate broker who specializes in helping older adults make housing decisions.

In some communities, a large fee is paid upfront, and some of it is returned when you leave. In others, people buy co-op shares they can sell later. There can also be monthly fees. If you’re buying in a new development, be sure to ask what happens to your investment if the project fails, or if you move away. Renting, of course, is a more flexible arrangement.

“It’s a big switch for most seniors, when we’re often living in our own homes for decades,” Ms. Ford said.

But living in these communities comes with benefits, too. “Your life gets more interesting,” Dr. Kaplan said.
